themes.name: Signals & Oscillations
themes.tagline: Deep dives into the circuits and physics that make the invisible world hum.

items.title: PLL - Voltage Controlled Oscillator - Source Coupled VCO
items.description:
This video explains the source-coupled VCO working principle. It is a particular kind of voltage controlled oscillator sometimes used in Phase looked loop for its low power dissipation.

Current starved Oscillator :  https://youtu.be/4yC7b6otcJ4
items.why_watch: A concise, focused walkthrough of the source-coupled VCO — a circuit topology that doesn't get much screen time compared to ring or LC oscillators. In under six minutes, it covers the working principle and why this design is favored in PLLs specifically for its low power draw, making it useful context if you're studying mixed-signal IC design or low-power RF systems.

themes.name: Arrow of Everything
themes.tagline: The universe has opinions about which way is forward — and they're weirder than you think.

items.title: Why You Can't Travel Backwards in Space
items.description: Turns out time isn't the only one with an arrow! Discover why traveling backwards in space is just as impossible as traveling backwards in time.
items.why_watch: The video makes a genuinely underexplored argument: that space, like time, has a directional arrow — and that moving 'backward' through space is constrained in ways that mirror the second law of thermodynamics. It's a short watch that reframes something you thought you understood about motion and symmetry, without requiring a physics background to follow along.

morning_soundtrack.title: U2 Announce New Album Carnaval de Luz Feat. Dolly Parton: Hear “Silencio”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The big dogs are back! It has been nearly nine years since U2 released Songs Of Experience , their last proper studio album of new music. This fall they will return with a 16th LP called Carnaval de Luz .
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Stadium-sized nostalgia colliding with rhinestone country magic, like finding an old postcard tucked inside a sequined jacket.

morning_soundtrack.title: Listen to Phoebe Bridgers’ New Song for A24 Film Primetime
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Bridgers stars in the Lance Oppenheim-directed movie opposite Robert Pattinson
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The kind of ache you feel watching city lights blur past a rain-streaked car window at 2 a.m.

morning_soundtrack.title: U2 Announce First Album in Nine Years
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Carnaval De Luz cut “Torn” features Dolly Parton’s last-recorded vocal performance
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: A bittersweet curtain call wrapped in arena reverb, like a farewell toast that goes quiet halfway through.

morning_soundtrack.title: Phoebe Bridgers Releases New Song “On Video” from Primetime Soundtrack: Stream
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The singer-songwriter is also making her acting debut in the new A24 film alongside Robert Pattinson. Phoebe Bridgers Releases New Song “On Video” from Primetime Soundtrack: Stream Karan Singh
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Delicate and cinematic, built for watching someone walk away through a sun-bleached parking lot.

morning_soundtrack.title: Vox: The Return of Our Monthly Vocal Jazz Column
morning_soundtrack.snippet: T he human voice has a million divergent roots, all growing wildly and wonderfully. Christopher Loudon knew that. The Toronto-based writer understood that so intimately …
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Like sitting alone in a warmly lit library while voices from every corner of the world drift softly past your ears.

morning_soundtrack.title: Jazz Pianist David Virelles Meets the Elders in Trio Imagination
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Trio Imagination's David Virelles is one of the most interesting pianists on the scene, conjuring music that integrates his heritage into inquiring contemporary jazz.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Ancestral memory rippling through a late-night piano trio, where every note feels both ancient and freshly discovered.

morning_soundtrack.title: Dallas Burrow Shows He’s From Texas in Hard-Earned Truths
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Like Dallas Burrow, Townes Van Zandt was a proud Texan, and one presumes he would be pleased to see his music celebrated as part of this brilliant Lone Star fest.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Dust-road honesty baked under a relentless Texas sun, for those who earn their feelings the hard way.

morning_soundtrack.title: Sova Beautifully Reinvents Her Sound on ‘Alight!’
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Sova's Alight! is filled with sonic possibilities, borrowing bits and pieces from jazz, classical, soul, and ambient experimentalism.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The feeling of a window thrown open on a cool morning — familiar air, but suddenly full of unexpected light.

morning_soundtrack.title: Truth About Vintage Amps, Ep. 171
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Skip is back from a long-overdue road trip and has tales to tell and amps to fix. We also hear about the Fretboard Summit’s vintage amp room (watch that baby Leslie video), Christopher Guest in the new Fretboard Journal and so much more. New Truth About Vintage Amps discount from Amplified Parts on all The post Truth About Vintage Amps, Ep.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Garage-scented nostalgia for people who hear a crackling tube amp and feel genuinely, inexplicably at home.

global_silver_linings.title: Australian Biologists Livestream A Remote Desert Waterhole and All its Wild Visitors
global_silver_linings.snippet: 1.2 miles from the nearest car park, down a track which few hikers ply, in a national park few will have the opportunity to visit, a lonely camera livestreams the comings and goings of a desert waterhole to the world. For the dingoes, wallabies, frogs, occasional feral cat, and even a wedge-tailed eagle who have […]
global_silver_linings.reason: Australian biologists are opening a window into the hidden rhythms of desert wildlife, letting anyone in the world witness the remarkable creatures that gather at a remote waterhole. It's a quiet reminder that wild places are still thriving — and that science can help us fall in love with them.

global_silver_linings.title: What went right this week: the good news that matters
global_silver_linings.snippet: Kosovo was cleared of landmines, Germany set a date for quitting oil, and a new species was discovered, plus more
global_silver_linings.reason: In a media landscape that often amplifies only the worst, a dedicated roundup of genuinely good news is a small act of resistance worth celebrating. It matters because hope, like a muscle, grows stronger the more we exercise it.

global_silver_linings.title: Millennial parents are pleading with Boomer grandparents to stop giving excessive gifts to grandkids
global_silver_linings.snippet: "I struggle to keep on top of tidying as it is, and this is a massive added challenge."
global_silver_linings.reason: Families are having honest, caring conversations about what children truly need — presence and meaning over piles of stuff. That kind of intergenerational dialogue is a healthy sign that values around childhood and consumption are thoughtfully evolving.

global_silver_linings.title: Nairobi Is Transforming Neglected Libraries Into Vibrant Civic Hubs
global_silver_linings.snippet: As Sunil Totti prepared for a job interview with an international tech firm recently, he was hit by a sudden anxiety: What if the electricity failed midway through? At home in Eastleigh, Nairobi, the power was notoriously unreliable. But that anxiety was quickly replaced by reassurance: “I know a place...
global_silver_linings.reason: Nairobi is proving that a neglected library can become a beating heart of community life, giving residents spaces to learn, connect, and imagine. When cities invest in shared public spaces, they invest in the dignity and potential of every person who walks through the door.

global_silver_linings.title: Ethiopia’s Green Legacy Initiative is turning citizens into foresters
global_silver_linings.snippet: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For most of the past century, Ethiopia was losing its forests. From the turn of the millennium to 2025, the country shed 560,000 hectares, about 2,160 square miles, of tree cover to agriculture, logging, and charcoal fuel. Then the government launched the Green Legacy Initiative in 2019, and citizens […] The post Ethiopia’s Green Legacy Initiative is turning citizens into foresters first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
global_silver_linings.reason: Ethiopia's Green Legacy Initiative has mobilised millions of ordinary citizens to plant billions of trees, turning reforestation from a government directive into a genuine grassroots movement. It's powerful proof that large-scale ecological restoration is possible when people are trusted to be part of the solution.

discovery_articles.title: Connell Lake Dam in Ketchikan, Alaska
discovery_articles.snippet: The Connell Lake dam is an imposing, almost gothic structure. Weather-worn and cracked in places, it blocks fish passage on Ward Creek. Frequently flagged by federal agencies like NOAA Fisheries, the dam cuts off miles of vital fish habitat.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: There's something quietly haunting about a dam described as 'gothic' that has spent decades cutting salmon off from miles of their ancestral habitat — a concrete monument to a forgotten priority. Federal agencies keep flagging it, yet it stands, weathered and stubborn, like a bad decision that refuses to admit itself.

discovery_articles.title: 14 Real Places That Haunt the Pages of Literature
discovery_articles.snippet: One of literature’s greatest gifts is its ability to transport us to other worlds: some utopian and fantastical, others dark and unnerving, scary and supernatural ... This guide is all about the latter (which are, arguably, much more fun). These are the novels, short stories, and novellas that get under your skin, that stay in your psyche long after you’ve put them down and returned to the world of the living.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The most unsettling thing about fiction's darkest places isn't that they were invented — it's that so many of them weren't. These are the real corners of the world that writers visited, felt something wrong in, and never quite shook.

discovery_articles.title: The Humble History of the Bedpan
discovery_articles.snippet: Over the past few centuries, inventors have tweaked the design of the receptacles here and there, but overall, not much has changed about the dependable medical supply
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Few objects have accompanied more moments of human vulnerability across centuries than the bedpan, yet its design has barely evolved — suggesting that some problems, however unglamorous, were essentially solved long ago and quietly left alone.

discovery_articles.title: Some Birdsongs Are More Pleasing to Human Ears Than Others. Higher-Pitched, Complex Calls Tend to Sound More Beautiful to Us
discovery_articles.snippet: In a new study, more than 80 participants rated the pleasantness of vocalizations made by 123 European bird species. Researchers then looked at the acoustic qualities of the most—and least—liked songs
discovery_articles.ferns_note: It turns out our aesthetic response to birdsong isn't purely cultural or poetic — there are measurable acoustic qualities that reliably move us, which raises the tender question of how long humans and birds have been, in some wordless way, tuned to each other.

discovery_articles.title: Fantastic Plants Spring from Taehyoung Maria Jeon’s Digital Illustrations
discovery_articles.snippet: Taehyoung Maria Jeon reimagines the plants cohabitating in her apartment, beginning with leaves and stems before venturing into surreal terrain.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Jeon doesn't invent her fantastical botanicals from nothing — she starts with the actual leaves on her windowsill, which makes the surreal feel like something your own houseplants might be quietly planning.

featured_read.title: Trump Should Stop Hosting Summits
featured_read.snippet: He’s turned them into a pointless ritual.
featured_read.blurb: A sharp-eyed argument that the diplomatic summit — once a charged, high-stakes occasion — has quietly collapsed into theater under Trump's watch. Worth reading if you've ever wondered why these gatherings feel like they're performing importance rather than achieving it.

reading_room.title: The Enduring Mystery of Annie Dillard
reading_room.snippet: Dillard kept much of her personal life carefully outside the scope of her nonfiction.
reading_room.blurb: Annie Dillard spent decades writing with ferocious intimacy about perception, nature, and God — while keeping her actual self almost entirely offstage, and this essay asks what that deliberate absence means for how we read her. A quiet puzzle about the line between a writer's vision and their life.

reading_room.title: Britain’s last great airship
reading_room.snippet: The remarkable engineering and tragic demise of the vessel that would end Britain’s dream to dominate the skies - by Aeon Video Watch on Aeon
reading_room.blurb: Behind Britain's ill-fated R101 airship lies a story of imperial ambition, engineering hubris, and the particular tragedy of a dream that almost worked. Set aside time to grieve something you never knew you'd lost.

reading_room.title: Gentle Exercise May be More Effective Than Medications at Managing Chronic Pain
reading_room.snippet: Side effects may include an improved mood
reading_room.blurb: The case here isn't that you should take a walk instead of a pill — it's that we've fundamentally misunderstood what chronic pain is and where it lives. A genuinely reorienting read for anyone who has wondered why nothing seems to touch it.

reading_room.title: A Tale of Two Trap Houses: Being Cuckooed Ruined My Friend’s Life—But Did It Then Help Save Him?
reading_room.snippet: "Drug gangs have moved off Britain’s streets and into vulnerable people’s homes. Addicts like my friend are easy targets, but the reality can be more complicated than it seems."
reading_room.blurb: "Cuckooing" — when drug gangs commandeer addicts' homes as operating bases — sounds like a clear-cut crime story, but this piece refuses that comfort, following one man's entanglement until victim and participant blur into something harder to judge. It's a portrait of how exploitation can, in the strangest of ways, also become a lifeline.

reading_room.title: Shrine: A Little Book About Paul Thek
reading_room.snippet: There is a photograph of Paul walking on a lawn and carrying a life-sized version of the cross. It appears to be quite heavy, made of wood. It can be seen to rest upon his shoulders.
reading_room.blurb: Paul Thek made art about mortality, flesh, and devotion — and this small, careful essay approaches him the same way he approached his subjects: with the seriousness of someone who actually believes in what they're looking at. A meditation on an artist too strange for easy canonization.

garden_note.note: There's a particular quality to the light at first light in late September Zürich — that low, amber wash over the Limmat valley that makes even the turning leaves look like they're lit from within. The dahlias and late sedums are holding on beautifully, but this morning carries the first real suggestion of something colder coming.

news.title: The Viral Beef Broth Bowl Is So Good, I Want It for Dinner Every Night
news.snippet: My screen time embarrasses me. I am very aware of how much time I spend (or, rather, waste) doomscrolling on social media. I just can’t give it up.
news.blurb: A beef broth bowl so deeply satisfying it's turning doomscrollers into devoted dinner planners — worth every minute of your screen time.

news.title: Why Chefs Love Cooking on Stainless Steel
news.snippet: Stainless steel cookware is experiencing a cultural renaissance. This isn’t to say that the genre of cookware ever disappeared, but, once upon a lockdown, it felt like an ad from a nonstick cookware brand was always a scroll away. Now that the dust has settled from the post-pandemic online shopping boom, the tides are shifting, and […]
news.blurb: Stainless steel is having its well-deserved moment in the spotlight, and this piece makes a compelling case for why chefs never really let it go.

news.title: The lure of the loo: how restaurant bathroom design went wild
news.snippet: Plush or pared back, flatteringly lit or full-on disco camp, a TikTokkable loo is now part of the hospitality experience Anthony Bourdain was typically forthright when it came to his expectations for the toilet facilities in a food business. “I won’t eat in a restaurant with filthy bathrooms,” wrote the late chef and author, in his seminal, turn-of-the-millennium memoir Kitchen Confidential. “This isn’t a hard call.
news.blurb: Restaurant bathrooms have become their own spectacle, and this delightfully absurd trend piece is the most fun you'll have reading about a loo.

recipe.title: Thin and Crisp Zucchini Scarpaccia
recipe.snippet: Thin and Crisp Zucchini Scarpaccia What to do with a boatload of zucchini? Scarpaccia, of course. This Italian flatbread emerges from the oven crisp at the edges, but soft and creamy inside.
recipe.blurb: A gorgeous late-summer Italian flatbread with crisp, golden edges and a soft, creamy centre — scarpaccia is the most elegant answer to a glut of zucchini, and it's wonderfully unfussy to make.

larder.seasonal_note: Zürich's Saturday markets at Bürkliplatz are quietly glowing right now with the last of the Zwetschgen — those deep-purple Swiss plums that make the most honest Zwetschgenwähe you'll bake all year. Pick up a kilo before the stone fruit disappears, and let the pastry cool long enough to have it properly, with a small coffee, before the morning mist lifts off the lake.

fern_data.greeting: U2 and Dolly Parton on the same album is either a fever dream or a dare — and somehow it's real. That's in here alongside the question of why you can't travel backwards in space, which turns out to be stranger and more personal than it sounds.
